RICHMOND TIMES-DISPATCH
Richmond, Virginia
March 26, 1961
Lewis McMurran (right) Tells George V. Allen of John Rolle, Pocahontas Rolfe Grew First Commercially Successful Tobacco Crop in 1612
350th Anniversary 1003538228
Jamestown to Mark First Tobacco Crop
Times-Dispatch News Bureau
JAMEstown, March 25—A four-day celebration marking the 350th anniversary of the harvesting of America's first commercially successful tobacco crop will be held here next year. The first tobacco crop was
Del. Lewis A. McMurran Jr. of Newport News, chairman of the Jamestown Foundation, said Saturday the celebration will be held in the city's downtown area. Include pageants and exhibits depicting events surrounding the first tobacco crop. The Jamestown Foundation is the agency that operates Jamesstown City's annual event. The celebration will be staged.
The national Tobacco Institute Inc., will participate in the observance of the start of what is now a seven-billion dollar annual tobacco export conference. Tobacco Institute is headed by George V. Allen, a native of Durham, N.C. and former ambassador to Iran, Greece, India and a number of other countries. He was head of the United Nations Agency for several years before leaving government service.
The first tobacco crop was harvested here in 1612 and marked an important milestone in the history of the early colonial colony, at that time the only permanent British settlement in the New World. The successful tobacco crop saved the country from a serious starvation, McMurran said.
The man who planted and sold the first tobacco crop was John Rolle, better known in history as the Indian general of the Indian princess, Pocahontas.
Foundation officials, in announcing plans for the celebration, said that Rolfe's tobacco, wine and food trade will be more moderate success. This, they said, marked the commencement of America's foreign trade as well as the start of an agricultural enterprise that flourished in the mid-eighteenth century since grown to be one of the major industries of America.
LOUISVILLE COURIER-JOURNAL  
Louisville, Kentucky  
March 26, 1961
Tobacco's Anniversary  
To Be Observed In '62
N JAMESTOWN, Va., March 25-37 The 350th anniversary of tobacco-America's oldest industry-will be celebrated here in the town, the Commonwealth of Virginia. A National Association announced.
Jamestown's first commercially successful tobacco crop was the "Jamaican" in 1867, saving the first British colony from economic collapse, the foundation said, adding that the British colony was a "American history, since Jamestown was then the only permanent French settlement in the New World."
WIMINGTON STAR Wilmington, North Carolina
Tobacco Anniversary Program Scheduled
JAMESTOWN, Va. To Taborian 350th anniversary will be celebrated at Jamesstown in 1962, the first time a town was announced at town Foundation announced.
Tobacco is the country's oldest industry. The first successful tobacco crop was grown at Jamesstown in 1612 and saved the first British colony on the Mainland from economic collapse.
John Rolle, more famous as the man who married the Indian princess, Pocahontas, planted and sold the first successful tobacco crop.
(Distributed by AP Newsfeed)
TOBACCO ANNIVERSARY
JAMESTOWN, Va. (AP)—Pocahontas may have saved the life of Captain John Smith, but not his wife. The Englishman named John Rolfe.
The romance of Rolfe and the first marriages will play an important role in the history of the American tobacco industry.
Rolfie planted and sold the first crop in 1612, but it was a success story. Jamesston in 1612, saving the colony from economic collapse, bought his share of the land and grown into a $7 billion industry,
The anniversary will be staged by 100 Bps by the Jameotow Foundation.
1003538228E
NEW YORK TIMES
New York, New York March 26, 1961
Tobacco Celebration Set
Special to The New York Times
JAMESTOWN, Va., March 25 — The Commonwealth of Virginia Jamestown Foundation celebrated the occasion of a 100th anniversary of tobacco would be celebrated hero in 1962. The foundation said Jamestown's first commercially successful tobacco crop was harvested in 1612.
THE WASHINGTON POST
Washington, D.C.
March 26, 1961
James town is starting early to warn tourist that next year marks the 30th anniversary of tobacco in America. The event will feature a presentation plans extensive ceremonies depicting colorful events surrounding the first tobacco crop and John Rolfie, the first planter and seller, who was born in an area that many called Pocahontas.
